where: the second line of the sheet's identity block — the role badge and 'Sign out' sitting on it together (identical in kiosk-menu, where the badge reads ADMIN)
finding: The proportion complaint is answered — the header is now shorter than the list and the destinations arrive first — but the line that paid for it put two objects from different registers on one baseline at the tightest gap in the panel. The role badge is a statement of fact and does nothing; it is also the only object in the whole sheet with a fill and a corner radius. 'Sign out' is the panel's one irreversible control and it has no container at all. So the shape that means 'press me' belongs to the label and the thing that is actually pressable is loose text beside it, and because they share a line at the sheet's smallest gap the eye takes them as one phrase — 'COUNSELOR Sign out' — rather than as a fact and an action. The reader's aim goes to the badge, which is inert, and the miss to the right of it is the one control on the screen that cannot be undone.
evidence: Counselor menu fold: email at ink-400 on its own line, then a row holding a filled ink-800 pill whose box runs x=16.5–87.5 and, 19.5px later, red text starting at x=107. The pill is the only filled rectangle between the sheet's top edge and the 'Kiosk' row; the button under 'Sign out' is fill-less and edge-less, its 44px box detectable only by touch. Squinting the row, the badge and the word read as a single left-aligned cluster.
direction: Stop the two sharing a line as peers. The role is an attribute of the identity and belongs with the email — beside it, or as plain text under it, with no container — which leaves the exit alone on its own line with the air its consequence deserves; or, if the pairing stays, the containment has to move from the label to the control so that the only bordered object in the sheet is the only pressable one. Not a colour change: the exit's chroma was set deliberately two rounds ago and should not be touched again.

where: the subordinating line under 'IF THE KIOSK STILL WAITS' and the three items below it
finding: The new sentence is supposed to demote the three causes underneath it, and nothing about its form says so. It is the same size, the same leading, the same measure and the same left edge as the items, it wraps to two lines exactly as they do, the list carries no markers to separate a member from a non-member, and the section spaces all five of its blocks — heading, caveat, three items — at one identical gap. So the caveat is bound to the heading no more tightly than the items are bound to each other, and what the reader sees is a run of four two-line paragraphs of which one happens to be a shade dimmer. The one line whose job is to say 'none of these is your problem yet' is drawn as the first of the things it is disowning. This matters more here than on the healthy page, because on the denied page the section is being read by somebody already looking for a cause.
evidence: Denied full frame: heading ink ends y=955.5, the caveat starts y=972 (16.5px); the caveat ends y=1002, item one starts y=1019 (17px) — the two gaps are the same. Markup: the section is a uniform gap-2 across h2, the caveat p and the ul, and the ul is gap-2 between li; caveat and items are both text-xs leading-relaxed, separated only by ink-500 against ink-400.
direction: Put the subordination in the composition, not only in the wording. Bind the caveat to the heading it qualifies — closer to it than the items are to each other, so it reads as the section's own preface — or give the three items a form the caveat does not share, so a reader scanning can see where the list begins. Worth noting alongside the desktop critic's call to lift the caveat's contrast: doing that alone would remove the last difference between it and the items and make this worse, so the two moves have to land together.

where: the page's two hairline rules — the one above 'IF THE KIOSK STILL WAITS' and the one above the '/kiosk is a self-serve screen…' small print (same pair on kiosk-setup and kiosk-setup-denied)
finding: The page's only two structural dividers are drawn identically and spaced differently. The first sits with equal air above and below it, so it reads as a break the layout chose. The second keeps the same air above and takes a third off below, so the small print starts closer to its rule than the section above did, and the rule looks less like a considered register change than like the point where the stack ran out of room. On a page whose whole shape is 'do the job, then reference, then footnote', the two moments that carry that shape should be built the same way, and a reader who cannot say why one break breathes and the other does not is reading an accident.
evidence: Counselor phone frame: rules at y=487 and y=693. Content clears the first by 24px above and 24px below (heading box top y=511); it clears the second by 24px above and 16px below (paragraph box top y=709). Markup: `border-t border-ink-800 pt-6` on the section, `border-t border-ink-800 pt-4` on the footer. The same 24/24 and 24/16 pair measures on kiosk-setup (rules y=415 and y=1066) and on kiosk-setup-denied.
direction: Pick one clearance for a full-measure rule and hold it on both, so the break itself is a constant and the change of register is carried by the type, which already does it — the footer is a size and two steps of the ramp below the section above it. If the footnote genuinely deserves to sit tighter than a peer section, the difference has to be big enough to read as a rank rather than as a rounding error.
